title: The Most Terrifying Survival Story Ever
fullText: In front of us is what looks like an ordinary photo from a ski vacation. A group of tourists, snow up to their knees, smiles, good vibes. But if you look closely at the bottom right corner of this photo, something isn't right. These are all the passengers of Uruguayan Air Force Flight 571. Their plane crashed in the middle of the Andes, the longest mountain range on the planet. They were stranded at an altitude of 3,600 m above sea level, where nighttime temperatures dropped to -30° C. And the nearest village was almost 100 km away across brutal, nearly impassable terrain. There were 45 people on board. 8 days after the crash, the search was officially called off. No one believed the passengers could still be alive. But at that exact moment, they were finishing their very last supplies. And they already knew what they were going to have to eat next. Today, you're going to find out just how far a human being is willing to go to survive. I'm going to tell you about the story of Flight 571 as if it all happened yesterday. Uruguay, a country that truly lives and breathes sports. Most of all, soccer and basketball. But since the 1960s, rugby has also been growing fast here. New clubs begin to appear. One of them, Old Christians. Just 8 years after its founding, the club had already become a two-time champion of Uruguay. The competition was amateur level, which meant the club didn't have much money. In 1972, Old Christians are invited to play a friendly match against the Chilean team, Old Boys. The game is away, so the club management starts looking for the cheapest way to fly. The Uruguayan Air Force agrees to transport the team. The prices are lower than civilian airlines, and for the military, it's a small side job. The day before departure, the players are told there are 10 empty seats on board, meaning they can bring friends or family members. 22-year-old player Nando Parrado decides to bring his mother, Eugenia Dolgay. She is a Ukrainian immigrant who fled to Uruguay during the years of Stalin's terror. Along with her, Nando's younger sister Susana is also coming to the match. October 12th, 1972. Flight 571 takes off from Montevideo Airport. On board are 40 passengers and five crew members. The aircraft commander is Colonel Julio César Ferradas, an experienced pilot with 5,000 flight hours under his belt. That's almost 7 months in the air without stopping. Beside him is the co-pilot, the less experienced Lieutenant Colonel Dante Héctor Lagurara. At some point, the weather deteriorates. A powerful cyclone forms over the Andes, and the pilots decide to wait it out in the Argentine city of Mendoza. By the next morning, the forecast looks a bit better. October 13th, Friday. Passengers board the plane again. Spirits are high. Someone jokes, "Maybe flying on such an unlucky date isn't the best idea." Of course, nobody takes it seriously. The plane takes off. The team needs to reach Santiago, the capital of Chile. Flying straight there isn't an option. To the west lie the Andes, mountains reaching nearly 7,000 m in height. Technically, the aircraft could climb that high, even higher, but it's fully loaded, and the weather outside isn't great. In short, it's extremely risky. So, the pilots choose a longer path. Fly south along the mountains, then west, [music] and only after that, north towards Chile's capital. Longer, more expensive, but safer. Commander Julio Ferradas had crossed the Andes 29 times. And today, he decides to let his co-pilot, Lugurada, get some practice. The aircraft is flying at 5,500 m passing near the Planchón Pass. >> [music] >> Thick clouds destroy visibility. The pilots are relying entirely on their instruments. At 7:31 p.m., Lugurada radios air traffic control. >> We expect to reach Curicó in 1 minute. >> But, that was impossible. Because from Planchón Pass to Curicó takes about 11 minutes of flight time. And Flight 571 had only been flying for about 3. Something is wrong. The navigation radar shows that Curicó is still 60 km away. The co-pilot doesn't notice, and the experienced commander doesn't double-check. 3 minutes later, Lugurada contacts the controller again. >> Passing over Curicó, turning north, requesting descent. >> The controller clears the plane to descend to 3,500 m. But, he has no radar, so he has no idea that Flight 571 is still over the Andes. And right now, the aircraft is beginning to descend straight towards the mountain. During the descent, the plane hits severe turbulence. The passengers' good mood evaporates. Although, not everyone yet understands how bad this really is. And then, they see it. A dark mountain range straight ahead. The pilots try to pull the aircraft up. The plane shakes violently, loses speed, and pitches nose up. A ground proximity warning alarm blares inside the cabin. Then the plane slams into rock again and again. The first impact tears off the right wing. Next, the entire rear section breaks away. The tail, two rows of seats, and the stabilizers. Three passengers, the navigator, and a flight attendant are killed. The remaining fuselage keeps moving forward until at 4,400 m altitude, a ridge rips off the left wing. A propeller slices through the fuselage, and two more passengers are thrown out. The main section of the aircraft hurdles another 700 m down a steep slope at 350 km/h. Then it crashes into a snowbank and doesn't stop instantly. During the crash, passenger seats rip free from the floor and slam into the forward bulkhead. The impact obliterates the cockpit and crushes the pilots against the instrument panel. Commander Julio Ferradas dies instantly. Along with him, 11 more passengers are killed, including the team doctor. The survivors find themselves stranded in the middle of snow-covered mountains at an altitude of 3,675 m. Many are injured. Some have bruises, some have broken bones, some have metal fragments embedded under their skin. Passengers with lighter injuries make their way to the cockpit. There they find Captain Ferradas dead and co-pilot Lagurara critically wounded. He's badly trapped and cannot move, and he keeps repeating one word, "Curicó." This confuses the passengers. They believe they made it to Chile, but in reality, the plane was still inside Argentina, deep in the heart of the Andes. Lagurara asks for a revolver, most likely to end his suffering. No one can bring themselves to give him a weapon. The next day, the co-pilot dies from his injuries. The rugby team Old Christians included many university students. Among them are Roberto Canessa and Gustavo Zerbino, both medical students. They weren't badly hurt, so in the hours after the crash, they got to work helping the injured, setting broken bones, using aircraft debris to fashion splints, and stabilizing shattered limbs. When darkness falls, the weather turns. A brutal cold sets in. Five people don't survive the night. >> [music] >> Some die from their injuries, others simply can't withstand the cold. There are also those who lie unconscious for hours. For example, Nando Parrado. During the crash, his skull is fractured. Lying beside Nando is his sister Susana, barely conscious and critically injured. Their mother, meanwhile, is among the first to die. By morning, only 28 people are still alive. Leadership naturally falls to the team captain, 25-year-old Marcelo Perez. He immediately stays level-headed and understands one thing. They will be searched for. Right now, the priority is simple. Survive and wait for rescue. Those who are able to work start clearing out broken seats and torn panels, turning the plane's fuselage into a crude shelter. They seal off the rear section with anything they can find, suitcases, twisted metal, and packed snow. This makeshift shelter is what will keep people alive when temperatures drop to minus 30° C. And then it finally feels like a miracle. A rescue plane flies overhead. People cheer, scream, and wave their arms desperate to be seen. But the pilots don't notice them. The white fuselage blends perfectly into the snow. Someone suggests writing SOS on the roof using lipstick. But there isn't enough. So instead, the passengers drag suitcases outside and arrange them in a giant cross on the snow. Three separate times, people watch rescue planes pass overhead. And all three times, the pilots never see them. At high altitude, every single breath delivers less oxygen than your body is used to. And that leads to hypoxia, oxygen starvation. You're suffocating even though there's plenty of air around you. For an unprepared person, this is a shock. Within minutes, shortness of breath appears along with a racing heartbeat, dizziness, nausea, and a pounding headache. This condition is known as altitude sickness. In some cases, it ends with swelling of the lungs and the brain, and that can be fatal. The passengers of Flight 571 lived in a warm, coastal climate, and now some of them were seeing snow for the first time in their lives. Their bodies could, in theory, fight altitude sickness, but adaptation requires time. And where would that time come from? One moment you're sitting inside a sealed, warm aircraft, and a minute later you're thrown into a cold, empty mountain. Too sudden, too extreme to adapt. On top of that, the stunning white landscapes around them were blinding, causing snow blindness. Their eyes burned from the ultraviolet light reflecting off the snow. It's similar to staring at a welding torch. Among all the wreckage, there's only about three pairs of sunglasses, so they have to improvise. Passengers take plastic sun visors from the cockpit and stitch them to bra straps with electrical wire. That way, everyone gets some form of primitive eye protection. The truth is, none of the passengers had any experience surviving in extreme conditions. But everyone wanted to live, so they learned fast. People stopped looking at objects for what they were meant to be, and started looking at what they could become. To stay warm, they used wool seat covers. Using scraps and debris, they built makeshift snowshoes. And then the passengers figure out how to get water. At first, driven by thirst, everyone simply eats snow. It ends badly, burning their throats and their lips. So, they decided to melt snow in the sun instead. The The search through the luggage for anything useful and find a camera. Dozens of photos will be taken with it, adding a strange layer of absurdity to the situation. I'm sure the passengers would have gladly traded for even a little food because real fear sets in when they count their remaining supplies. Eight chocolate bars, three jars of jam, one can of mussels, one can of almonds, a few candies, dates, dried plums, and several bottles of wine. This won't last long. All they can do now is hope for help. On the third day after the crash, rugby player Nando Parrado regains consciousness and wakes up to the horrifying realization that his mother is already gone. He stays by his injured sister's side, never leaving her. But her condition keeps getting worse. Soon, she dies, too. Yet, instead of breaking down, Nando does the opposite. He finds the strength to support others. He desperately wants to make it out of here alive. But, surviving without food is almost impossible. The group carefully divides their tiny rations among everyone. No one ever feels full. And within a week, even that food is gone. All around them, only snow and rock. No plants, no animals, nothing. Some wonder if the seat cushions might be stuffed with straw, something, anything they could eat. They cut them open and inside is cheap foam. Then passengers try chewing on leather from belts and shoes, but the leather is treated with chemicals and it makes them violently ill. Under normal conditions, a person can survive without food for about 2 months. But in the mountains, the body burns through its reserves far faster. The medical students among them know that without protein, the body cannot function properly and will begin to break down rapidly. And on the 10th day after the crash, some of the passengers realize there is, in fact, food all around them. When it comes to survival, you look at everything differently. The idea that we would have to eat our dead friends was terrifying, but it wouldn't go away. Many of us had the same thought at the same time. All of the deceased passengers had been buried in the snow near the plane wreckage. The cold was so intense that the bodies did not decompose. They could be used as food. Obviously, not everyone accepted this idea. The passengers of flight 571 were mostly friends and relatives, not strangers. And many of them were devout Catholics who feared that consuming human flesh would condemn them to hell. Even the people who first voiced the idea hated it. At first they suggested starting with the pilot since the crash happened because of him. But by day 11, everyone understood that there was truly no other choice. That moment came when the passengers found a small radio. They turned it on and learned that the search and rescue operation had been called off. From that point on, survival became a pact between them. If one of them died, the others would use the body as food. Medical student Roberto Canessa used a sharp shard of glass to slice the flesh into thin strips. The group decided that the same people would always handle this task so others would not know exactly whose body they were eating. Nando Parrado protected the bodies of his mother and sister. Relatives were not to be touched. They tried not to eat the meat raw. Instead, they dried and cured it under the sun. Some compared this to the Eucharist, the transformation of bread and wine into the body and blood of Jesus. Greater love has no one than this, than to lay down one's life for one's friends. Protein gives them back some strength. A small group of rugby players head out to scout the area around the wreck. But without proper equipment, they can't go very far. The mood in camp constantly shifts. One moment it feels like everything will be okay, and the nightmare will soon be over. And the next, that everything is hopeless, [music] and no one is coming to save them. Even so, the group's leaders never stop lifting people's spirits up. Everyone supports one another, even though in truth, no one knows what to do next. The most terrifying thought is the future. What happens when the bodies are gone? But, on October 29th, 16 days after the crash, that question answers itself. Another night, as always, the passengers huddle inside the fuselage to keep warm. And then, an avalanche slams into them. Snow packs the cabin almost to the ceiling. Eight people suffocate. Among them, the last woman, Liliana Methol. She had become a nurse and a mother figure to the young men. Her body, too, is declared off-limits. Along with Liliana, the snow takes Gustavo Nicolich, the first person who encouraged the passengers after learning the search had been called off. But, the most painful loss is the group's leader, the captain of the Old Christians team, Marcelo Perez. Nando Parrado is the first to realize that under the snow, oxygen inside the plane is running out fast. He grabs a metal pole and smashes a hole through the cockpit windshield. Then, together with others, he rushes to dig out their friends. In the end, that leaves 19 survivors. And as brutal as it sounds, the avalanche saved their lives. First, the thick layer of snow turns the fuselage into a solid shelter from the freezing cold and the storm that hasn't stopped for 3 days. And second, the group now has more food. The avalanche shatters their last remaining hope of rescue. Now everyone understands the only way to survive is to climb over the mountain and go for help. Before he died, the co-pilot kept repeating one word, Curicó. That's why the passengers were convinced that Chilean villages were somewhere nearby, just a few kilometers to the west. But reality was far more brutal. The actual distance to those villages was around 80 to 90 kilometers. >> [music] >> The snow was slowly beginning to melt. Summer was approaching. See, these events took place between October and December of 1972. For us up here, [music] that's fall and winter. But in the Southern Hemisphere, where Chile and Argentina are, it's spring and summer. That seasonal shift gives them a dangerous sense of opportunity. So the group decides they have to go. Roberto Canessa, Nando Parrado, and Antonio Vizintín are the strongest amongst the survivors. They're given double portions of meat, the warmest clothing, and are freed from daily duties. They're preparing for the hardest challenge of their lives. At first, the men plan to head west towards Chile. But that route means climbing a massive mountain. So on November 15th, they choose to go east instead. The passengers believe the valley will eventually curve west and lead them to people. After about a kilometer and a half, the rugby players discover the tail section of the plane. Inside are fragments of a long-forgotten life, a box of candy, frozen meat [music] patties, a bottle of rum, Coca-Cola, cigarettes, spare clothes, medicine, [music] comic books, and batteries. Night is approaching, so the men decide to sleep right there, inside the tail of the aircraft. >> [music] >> They build a fire to keep warm and stay up late reading comic books. In the morning, the rugby players wake up in good spirits. They start walking again. Ahead of them lies a descent to the east, but the weather quickly turns worse. On the second night, the team nearly freezes to death. Pushed to the edge, they're forced to turn back and return to the tail section of the plane. There, they remember the batteries, and an idea takes shape. Connect the plane's radio and send out an SOS signal. But, the 24-kg batteries turn out to be far too heavy to carry. So, the men decide to do the opposite. They bring the radio to the tail instead. >> [music] >> However, the aircraft radio requires 115 volts of alternating current. Well, the batteries provide only 24 volts of direct current. From the very beginning, this plan is doomed. There's simply no way to make it work. And eventually, the men return to the group. Back at the fuselage, people die again. Two passengers are taken by infection, and one, Numa Turcatti, simply cannot bring himself to eat the meat. His body grows weaker and slowly stops fighting for life. There's no other choice. They have to prepare for another expedition. Only this time, they must prepare properly. [music] At one point, the group's radio receiver picks up good news. The Uruguayan military has resumed the search. They aren't searching for survivors, but for bodies. Still, either way, the chances of being found have increased. They just need to wait. The biggest problem is that none of the passengers have ever gone mountaineering before. And the higher you climb, the harder it becomes to breathe. So, to avoid freezing at night, they sew a sleeping bag for the expedition. It's made from insulation taken from the fuselage, wires, and waterproof fabric from the plane's air conditioning system. The bag fits three people, who must also keep each other warm with their own body heat. Once again, the same three men prepare for the trek. But this time, Canessa hesitates. He's troubled by the fact that none of the other passengers are willing to join the expedition. Parrado pushes him. They have to go now while they still have strength and while the weather allows it. Nando is in a hurry for another reason. The bodies they use for food are slowly running out. And he doesn't want to wait for the moment to come when they have to turn to his mother and his sister. On December 12th, 60 days after the crash, the trio leaves the camp. >> [music] >> Parrado dresses like a human cabbage, a wool hat, a hood, three sweaters, several pairs of jeans, boots, and four pairs of socks wrapped in plastic bags. They take food for 3 days. No proper gear, no maps, no compass, no mountaineering experience. All they have are long aluminum poles. They begin climbing the ridge from an altitude of 3,664 m. Straight up a steep slope at an angle of 30° to 60°. The rugby players think they can reach the top in 1 day. But in places, they sink knee-deep into sun-softened snow. And the thin air makes altitude sickness even worse. >> To take a single step, I had to breathe at least five times. But we kept climbing towards the summit. People down below called us brave, but what drove us forward was fear. >> On the first night, the trio barely finds a place to lay out the sleeping bag. It's a rocky ledge at the edge of an abyss. A piercing wind is blowing. But the sleeping bag has been sewn well, and it does its job. The next day, the climb is even harder. From base camp, the remaining passengers watch for 3 days as three black dots slowly crawl upwards. On the third morning, Canessa stays the sleeping bag to conserve energy. Vizentin and Parrado move towards an almost vertical 100-m wall covered in snow and ice. They managed to reach the ridge at an altitude of 4,503 m. What waits for them is a crushing disappointment. Instead of green valleys of Chile, they see endless snow-covered peaks. No signs of life anywhere. Disheartened, they climb back down to Canessa to make camp for the night. They're surrounded by breathtaking scenery. In the evening, after a tiny sip of rum they found in the tail of the plane, Parrado says, "Roberto, imagine how beautiful this would be if we weren't walking dead men." The alcohol warms them up slightly. Surprisingly, their spirits are still holding up. In spite of everything, they decide that they have to keep moving. The rugby players make an agreement. Vizentin will return to camp so that Canessa and Parrado will have enough food for the long journey ahead. In the morning, the Old Christians forward sits on a seat like a sled and within an hour slides all the way back down to the plane. Now, Nando Parrado and Roberto Canessa are alone. They climb up another mountain ridge. They see the same lifeless emptiness. For a moment, they stare silently into the distance. Then Canessa thinks, "We're dead." But Parrado notices a valley and two peaks without snow. He says, "Maybe we're doomed, but I'd rather walk towards death than wait for it." Canessa agrees. "We're friends, Nando. We've been through so much. Now, let's go die together." After those words, they descend into the valley, into the unknown. >> For 7 days, Parrado and Canessa walked deeper into Chile. Eventually, they reach a narrow valley and discover the source of a small river. The men follow the water and at last, the snow is gone. The cold is no longer their main threat. On one hand, that's good. But now, the meat begins to rot. Every single piece has to be rationed. On top of that, Roberto Canessa's dysentery grows worse. With each passing day, they're able to walk less and less. And then, a miracle. The men spot an empty soup can lying in the grass, a sign of civilization. On the ninth day, they find cow manure and they are overjoyed. And then, they see the cows themselves. By this point, Canessa is barely holding on. Before the crash, he weighed over 90 kg. Now, just 44. Another evening falls. Nando Parrado goes out to collect firewood. And on the other side of the river, he sees a man. Parrado shouts to him, but the roar of the water swallows his words. But the man across the river notices Parrado anyway and shouts back a single word. Tomorrow. The next day, the man really does return. His name is Sergio Catalan, a local shepherd. Sergio writes a note, ties it to a rock along with a pencil, and throws it across the river. Parrado writes back. Our plane crashed in the mountains. I'm Uruguayan. We have been walking for 10 days. I have an injured friend. There are still 14 wounded people at the plane. We need to get out of here quickly, but we don't know how. We have no food. We are very weak. Will you come for us, please? We can barely walk. Where are we? Parrado throws the note back across the river. Canessa reads it and gestures that he understands everything. He tosses the rugby players bread and cheese, then rides on horseback for 10 hours towards the nearest town. Along the way, Sergio meets another shepherd and asks him to go to the men and take them to the village. Canessa keeps riding. He flags down a truck and asks the driver to take him to a police station. From there, police pass the information to the 19th infantry regiment. The military then contacts Chilean Army headquarters in Santiago. That's how the impossible becomes real. News of survivors from flight 571 reaches the capital. Within hours, it's on every major channel in the country. Back at the camp near the wrecked fuselage, the remaining survivors celebrate, too. Their radio picks up the news. No one can believe that Parrado and Canessa actually made it to civilization. Meanwhile, the two men are brought on horseback to a small town where they are fed and allowed to rest. The rugby players themselves can hardly believe what they've accomplished, climbing 839 m up, descending 1,425 m, and walking more than 50 km across brutal terrain. But, they don't rest for long because others are still out there. They have to go back. They have to save the rest. [music] The Chilean Air Force dispatches helicopters flying towards Parrado and Canessa's location. The men trace an approximate route to their camp on a map, and on December 22nd, two helicopters finally reach it. Each helicopter can only carry half of the survivors at once, so four rescuers agree to stay behind overnight with the others. And at dawn on December 23rd, they returned to pick up the second group of passengers. In total, they spent 72 days trapped in the frozen mountains. After that, everyone is transported to hospitals in Santiago. Once there, they're treated for altitude sickness, dehydration frostbite scurvy and extreme exhaustion. I don't know about you, but these images still send chills down my spine. Out of 45 people, only 16 survive. And that alone feels like a miracle. Because before this, every plane crash in the Andes had ended in complete tragedy. That's why the news reporters speak about the rescue with optimism and awe. But before long, journalists begin asking a different question. What did they eat? Rescuers were the first to notice human remains scattered around the wreckage. But since the crash happened on Argentine territory, the Chileans decide to leave the matter to Argentina. The military only photographs the bodies, marks their locations on a map, and returns home. In the first days, the passengers of flight 571 hide the truth. They tell the press they survived on food from the plane and later on local plants. The survivors want to first explain the cannibalism to their families, but rumors spread far too fast. People begin claiming the survivors killed the weakest among them for food. On December 23rd, the story appears in newspapers around the world, except in Uruguay. And when two Chilean newspapers print front page photos of a partially eaten human leg, the passengers can no longer stay silent. They hold a press conference where they explain the pact they had made. After death, each person would donate their body so the others could survive. And most people respond with compassion. The families of the dead do not condemn the survivors. Instead, they support them. All public outrage finally fades after a statement from the Catholic Church. It declares that the passengers of flight 571 will not be damned for cannibalism because they did not kill. They were simply trying to survive. After the rescue operation, life had to begin again for the 16 survivors. They were all young men who had lived through unimaginable horror. And finding the strength to keep living is a battle in itself. According to the latest information we found, out of the 16 survivors, 12 are still alive today. After everything they endured, some of them even managed to return to professional sports. You might be surprised, but the Old Christians rugby team already won the Uruguayan national championship the very next year, in 1973. They'd lost half their squad to the Andes, yet the tragedy turned the club into a symbol. Top players wanted to join a team that had shown such incredible strength of spirit. In this photo, Nando Parrado and Roberto Canessa are playing rugby. It was taken in April 1973, just 4 months after their rescue. Every year on December 22nd, the day the rescue operation began, the survivors gather together. They bring their children with them. They show each other that their survival truly meant something. And in the 21st century, veterans of Old Christian even played several commemorative matches against Chilean teams. Once, the kickoff was taken by Sergio Catalán, the same shepherd who threw Nando and Roberto a stone with a note and a pencil tied to it. Sadly, on February 11th, 2020, he passed away. Sergio lived to be 91 years old. Those who survived later described their experiences in autobiographies. There are many motivational quotes in these books, but one from Roberto Canessa truly stuck with me. We should be more thankful that we receive much more than we need, and we do much less than we can. So, remember these words when things feel impossible. Thank you for sticking around until the end. Feel free to drop a like and subscribe if you enjoyed this video. Comment below what moment in history you'd like to hear from us or want us to cover next. For more exclusive content, be sure to follow us on Patreon. This has been Yesterday. We'll see you next time.
fullTextVi: Trước mặt chúng tôi là thứ trông giống như một bức ảnh bình thường từ một chuyến trượt tuyết kì nghỉ. Một nhóm du khách, tuyết ngập đến đầu gối, mỉm cười, tâm trạng vui vẻ. Nhưng nếu bạn nhìn kỹ vào góc dưới bên phải của bức ảnh này, có điều gì đó không đúng. Đây đều là hành khách trên Chuyến bay 571 của Không quân Uruguay. Máy bay của họ bị rơi ở giữa dãy Andes, dãy núi dài nhất trên hành tinh. Họ bị mắc kẹt ở độ cao 3.600 m so với mực nước biển, nơi ban đêm nhiệt độ giảm xuống -30° C. Và ngôi làng gần nhất cách đó gần 100 km, có địa hình khắc nghiệt, gần như không thể vượt qua. Có 45 người trên tàu. 8 ngày sau vụ tai nạn, cuộc tìm kiếm chính thức bị đình chỉ. Không ai tin các hành khách vẫn còn sống. Nhưng vào đúng thời điểm đó, họ đang hoàn thành những nguồn cung cấp cuối cùng. Và họ đã biết trước mình sẽ phải ăn gì tiếp theo. Hôm nay, bạn sẽ tìm hiểu xem con người sẵn sàng đến mức nào đi để tồn tại. Tôi sẽ kể cho các bạn nghe về câu chuyện Chuyến bay 571 như thể nó tất cả đã xảy ra ngày hôm qua. Uruguay, một đất nước thực sự sống và hít thở thể thao. Nổi bật nhất là bóng đá và bóng rổ. Nhưng kể từ những năm 1960, bóng bầu dục cũng phát triển nhanh chóng ở đây. Các câu lạc bộ mới bắt đầu xuất hiện. Một trong số họ, những Cơ đốc nhân cũ. Chỉ 8 năm sau khi thành lập, câu lạc bộ đã hai lần trở thành nhà vô địch của Uruguay. Cuộc thi diễn ra ở cấp độ nghiệp dư, nghĩa là câu lạc bộ không có nhiều tiền. Năm 1972, các Old Christian được mời đến chơi một trận giao hữu với người Chile đội, Những chàng trai già.
